speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE TO ENSURE FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing a measure to be known as "The Canada Full Employment Act", and that consideration should be given to including in the said proposed measure, inter alia, the following provisions; (a) a clearcut recognition by parliament of the importance of full employment as a national policy; (b) a declaration that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the steps that are necessary to provide and maintain a full

employment economy; (c) the establishing of a council of economic advisers, empowered to make regular reports containing economic analyses and projections based on objective research, such reports to be made public; and (d) a requirement that there be an annual report to parliament, by the minister responsible for the administration of the act, on measures taken under its provisions, with opportunity for scrutiny and debate, so that parliament might make sure that the purposes of the proposed act are fulfilled.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion, as its terms indicate, asks that consideration be given to the enacting of a statute to be known as "The Canada Full Employment Act". I believe that this is the first time such a proposal has been formally placed before the House of Commons. If one has in mind the batting average of private members' motions and private members' bills, I suppose I should not be too hopeful that it will pass in the hour allotted to it. However, hope does spring eternal, and because of the great importance of the subject matter of this motion I dare to hope that the house might give its approval to it. If this does not happen today I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that it will happen some day; that the day will come when there will be on our statute books an act of this description. When that day comes a full employment act, or a guaranteed employment act, will rank with what I hope by that time is a proper bill of rights, and with other such pieces of legislation as amongst the most important items on our statute books.
Mr. Speaker, when Canada first came into being in 1867, and when the parliament of Canada was created by the British North America Act of that day, it was felt that the role of government was somewhat limited. It was the job of parliament and of the government to arrange for the administration of essential services, to provide for the defence of the country, to organize the postal services, and things of that sort, but it was the feeling of that day that the functions of the government should be limited. In the 95 years since confederation the picture has changed considerably. The number of responsibilities which fall to parliament and government has grown, and will continue to grow in the years which lie ahead. In particular we have multiplied the services, the organization and provision of which we recognize as the responsibility of government. We have gone a great way, even in the political lifetimes of many of us in this chamber, in the field of social security in the enactment of measures which were visionary and idealistic a generation or two ago. Things which are thought to be beyond the responsibility of government are now on our statute books. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that 27507-3-173
Labour Conditions
one of the next areas into which we must move, and move with determination, is the question of seeing to it that full employment is provided for our people. The fact that this sort of thing is happening is, of course, supported by certain pieces of legislation which are before this parliament. The rules prevent me from referring to them in any detail, but I think it would be in order for me to say in passing that the very fact that we are discussing such items as an Atlantic development board and a national economic development board is an admission by the government and this parliament that there is a job now for both government and parliament to do in the economic field.
Mr. Speaker, we feel that what is required is far more than is suggested in these other pieces of legislation which are before this house. We think that something comparable to a bill of rights, something comparable to the assertion that there are basic things which belong to the people of this country, should be done in the field of guaranteeing full employment. That is why we suggest in the terms of this resolution that this house should ask the government to give consideration to the advisability of bringing such a measure before parliament. As suggested in the resolution, we propose that such a statute should include a number of things. In the first place, it should include a clearcut recognition by parliament of the importance of full employment as a national policy. When we reach the point where we accept that responsibility as a parliament, we will be able to do something about it, rather than just hoping that private industry, under benefits and arrangements made by the government, will do the job for us. I suggest this becomes just as important a responsibility and as important a function for the parliament of Canada now as the social services we provide, as the defence of the nation, as our diplomatic policy, and as our basic human rights. In fact, one of the things missing in the discussion which took place in this house during the last parliament on the bill of rights was the question of the important economic and social rights which belong to our people. Therefore, we feel that parliament should declare quite clearly and in forthright manner that we do not leave this responsibility to private sectors of the economy, that we do not leave it to chance. We accept it as parliament's responsibility to maintain a policy of full employment.
A second recognition which we feel should be in a full employment act or a guaranteed employment act should be a declaration that it

Labour Conditions
is the responsibility of the federal government to take the steps necessary to provide and maintain a full employment economy. Here again it will be noted that we are asking for a good deal more than that which is proposed in other items of legislation before this parliament at the present time. We ask not just for boards or committees to discuss these things; we ask for recognition in a statute of parliament that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the necessary steps which will provide full employment for our people.
A third proposal which we think should be in a statute of this kind would be one for the setting up of a council of economic advisers. This is something far more than is proposed with regard to a certain board being discussed under another item. We feel that this council of economic advisers should be empowered to make regular reports containing economic analyses and projections based on objective research, and that all these reports made by the council of economic advisers should be made public.
The fourth of the items which we suggest should be in such a statute would be the requirement that there should be an annual report to parliament, by the minister responsible for the administration of the act, of measures taken under its provisions so that there would be an opportunity for scrutiny and debate, to the end that the House of Commons will be able to make sure that the purposes of the act are being fulfilled. In other words, what we are suggesting is that concern for the economy or concern that the economy produce full employment be put at the very centre of our responsibilities as the elected representatives of the people of this country. If the House of Commons will take this responsibility and if we will get down to business and do the things which are necessary in terms of economic planning, enlarging the public sector, and greater public ownership, in order to provide full employment, on that basis we believe we can do just about all the things we feel we should be doing for our people.
For example, we know that we have a long way to go in this country in terms of providing adequate housing. We know that we have a tremendous way to go in terms of providing health care for all our people. A moment ago I spoke about the progress we have made in the field of social security. However, we have a great deal to do yet in that field. We cannot do these things as we should do them while we are suffering from unemployment and while we are failing to produce the wealth or the goods and the services which we have the capacity to bring into being.

However, if we provide full employment, if we make that responsibility a major concern of the parliament and the government of Canada, we can really fill the bill in terms of housing, health, security, education and all the things our people need.
There is one other area which concerns us greatly today, namely our contribution to building up the economies of the underdeveloped countries of the world. We know that in this way and in this way only can we achieve and maintain permanent peace. In order to do this, in order to make a significant contribution-and I suggest that it should be a massive one-to the development of underdeveloped countries, it will be necessary to have full employment and to have people at work producing goods and services on a scale far beyond anything in existence in Canada at the present time. In other words, we are concerned not just with taking up the slack so that there will not be unemployment and the suffering that goes with it; we are concerned about the kind of full, effective and efficient employment that produces goods and services which will provide a good economy and a good standard of living for our people and which will enable us in Canada to make a significant contribution to improving the conditions of life for people the world around and in so doing will enable us to make a significant contribution toward the peace of the world.
So, Mr. Speaker, I emphasize as I did at the start the fact that this is the kind of statute that would put concern for full employment at the centre of our parliamentary responsibilities; it is comparable to a bill of rights or to those thinks that belong in the basic constitution of a nation such as ours. This kind of statute is one that sooner or later we must have. Because of the present need for action in our own time we hope that something may be done about this matter at an early date.
By the very nature of things this resolution cannot put the proposed statute on the statute books; it is put forward as a private members' resolution which asks that the government give consideration to the advisability of taking this course. Because of its importance I hope that there will be a reasonable amount of discussion of this proposal but that the house may see fit to endorse the motion and ask the government to consider this extremely important matter.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE TO ENSURE FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who just spoke, I noted one of his remarks in which he indicated, if I may paraphrase his words, that this was the first time something of this nature had been brought before this house. I would suggest that this is not really the first

time something of this nature has been before us. Back in 1945, in a somewhat different form, the Liberal government of that day brought down a famous white paper on employment and income which laid out the chart for Canada's progress in the post-war years until 1957. In that white paper it was set forth as a matter of government policy that full employment was an aim of government for the Canadian people. I quote from page 1:
The central task of reconstruction in the interests of the armed services and civilians alike, must be to accomplish a smooth, orderly transition, from the economic conditions of war to those of peace and to maintain a high and stable level of employment and income. The government adopts this as a primary object of policy... In setting as its aim a high and stable level of employment and income, the government is not selecting a lower target than "full employment".
In summarizing, at page 23, the various policies set forth in this famous white paper, it concluded as follows:
In this paper, the government has stated unequivocally its adoption of a high and stable level of employment and income, and thereby higher standards of living, as a major aim of government policy.
In this white paper were set forth policies which stimulated the expansion of the Canadian economy and created jobs for hundreds of thousands of soldiers returning from the war. They included policies with regard to low interest rates, incentives for private investment, public investment, the stimulation of housing and slum clearance. When we look at the record of Canada between 1945 and 1957 we can see the record of achievement which resulted from this clear statement of policy in this famous white paper in 1945. We had a rate of growth that made us the envy of the world. We had a rate of employment that certainly ranked with the best in the world either before or since.
I do not think I need to dwell at this time on what has happened since 1957. The Canadian people know only too well the differences between the years before 1957 and the years after, the lag in economic growth, in fact the outright decay and stagnation of our economic life, the startling increase in our rate of unemployment which, unfortunately, at times put us among those countries with the highest rates of unemployment in the world.
It is true that the time has come once again for a further clear cut and definitive statement of policy that full employment shall once again be a major aim of the government of Canada. But if once again we adopt this as a policy, I suggest that we must make sure that the policy is carried out in ways which continue to provide freedom of choice 27507-3-173i
Labour Conditions
for workers in going from job to job, freedom of movement for those workers who want to move. As a basic aim, however, this aim of full employment is still as valid today as it was in 1945. Unfortunately, in spite of the manner in which this has been brought most forcefully to the attention of the people of Canada and the manner in which the people of Canada have brought their dissatisfaction with this state of affairs to the attention of the government, a dissatisfaction expressed most forcibly in the rather startling decline in seats now held by the government compared with after the previous election, we still see, in looking at the dominion bureau of statistics publication dealing with the labour force, that the unemployment rate in November of this year was 5.2 per cent compared with 5.4 per cent in November, 1961.
I mention this not only to draw to the attention of the house something which is all too obvious to all too many people in this country, but also to point out that statements of policy, whether in a white paper or in an act of this parliament as suggested by the last speaker, are really not enough. There has to be the will and desire to carry out and implement policies based on the basic policy to which I have referred. The bill of rights, to which reference was made by the hon. member who just spoke, is a good example of this particular point. It is on the statute books and reads very well, but we still do not have the achievement of all the basic rights that are supposed to be embodied in it. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say it even appears from time to time that the present government, which seems to take such pride in the passage of that act, ignores its precepts in carrying on their activities. Therefore I suggest that if you have an act of this type on the statute books it must be accompanied by the will and desire to carrry out the appropriate policies foreshadowed in a piece of legislation of this type.
I do not think it is necessary to discuss in detail the various parts of the resolution. Some of them are now before the house in other forms. In passing, however, I must say that I was interested to note the remarkable similarity of this resolution to the employment act of 1946 of the United States. I do not say this by way of criticism particularly. Certainly we have not reached the stage of perfection in this country that we can afford not to get good ideas from other places in the world, but I thought I should remark upon that in passing. In any event, Mr. Speaker, measures of this type are already before the house in other forms in one way or another.

Labour Conditions
But I do want to conclude my remarks by pointing out that full employment remains and even more than ever is a basic policy of the Liberal party today. Full employment in an expanding economy will be the first aim of the new Liberal government. So we stated during the last election, so we stated previously; and I do not think we can reiterate this basic principle of policy too often because I am sure we will have the first opportunity to put this policy into effect.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Muir (Cape Breton Norih and Vicloria):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE TO ENSURE FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to speak briefly on this motion. At the outset let me say that there is reference to such an act in the submission presented to the cabinet by the Canadian Labour Congress in March of 1962. It is in substantially the same terms as the resolution now before us in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). However, there is no reference to such an act in the latest brief of the Canadian Labour Congress presented to the government last week. Perhaps in the interval they have had second thoughts about the efficacy of such a bill, or perhaps its omission from their latest brief may be connected with the fact that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is no longer executive vice president of the Canadian Labour Congress. In any case, although the motion leaves a lot to be desired it is all we have to go on at the present time and the present discussion must, therefore, be based on the terms which the hon. member has seen fit to place before the house.
In a general way, before examining in detail the terms of the proposed bill, it is perhaps useful to consider the general principle of a bill to legislate full employment. It is, of course, in line with socialist thinking that by simply waving a legislative wand, as it were, all problems of the economy can be cured. Perhaps this is what they mean when they talk about planning, that it is merely a matter of putting legislation into effect to bring about those desirable objectives which we would all like to achieve and to eliminate all problems which are currently the lot of troubled humanity. Would it were that easy.
There are some problems that cannot be solved simply by saying "let there be light". At least, in the past they have only been solved in that manner through the possession of those divine faculties which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has not yet given satisfactory evidence of possessing. In effect this bill, if passed, would simply say, "let there be full employment", and the minister would be in the position of reporting from time to time on the extent to which this injunction was being realized.

I have strong doubts, Mr. Speaker, that simply by passing a bill of this nature full employment can be created. If it were only that simple then, of course, all our problems would be over. If the bill obviously cannot accomplish what it sets out to accomplish, then what is its purpose? I am afraid that it would become simply another case of window dressing.
When you examine the resolution closely, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the hon. member has included a number of provisions which he would like to have in the proposed bill. They are in summary: First, clearcut recognition by parliament of the importance of full employment as a national policy. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is not an hon. member in this house who does not favour full employment as a national policy. The only possible exception might be the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) who, I believe in the course of some of his writings, has stated that a certain level of unemployment "helps to keep the economy flexible". That statement can be found on page 421 of the Gordon commission report. With that possible exception every member of the house, I am sure, has favoured the principle of full employment.
This is a proposal that, when looked at closely, will not provide one single job for one single Canadian, and from that point of view simply reduces itself to a form of legislative wishful thinking. I do not think parliament should be asked to approve legislation dealing with wishful thinking. I would suggest that if the hon. member has some definite and positive, some concrete and practical proposition to provide jobs, then he should bring it forward. Were he to do so, I feel he would get quite a bit of support. I do not think it can be done by the embodiment of a pious platitude in the form of parliamentary legislation. When the time comes that parliament indulges in this sort of phraseology as a substitute for hard, legislative action, then we will have gone a long way towards losing our effectiveness.
The second provision would require a declaration to the effect it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the steps that are necessary to provide and maintain a full employment economy. This is another of those vague generalizations. I would have been far more eager to support the hon. member's motion if he had told us specifically what those necessary steps are. I would contrast this with the program of the present government which, right from the beginning, has accepted fully the fact there was an unemployment problem in this country, has accepted fully its constitutional responsibilities, and has evolved specific measures to

deal with the problem. I would say that nine out of ten of those measures receive the unanimous support of this house when brought before parliament.
I would point out to the hon. member that the responsibility in this field is not solely that of the federal government. The federal government can act and has acted. Under our constitutional system, there remains a substantial field of provincial jurisdiction. I believe it was the present Liberal premier of Quebec who maintained during his 1960 campaign that unemployment was the responsibility of the province. I do not know what his stand is now since, unfortunately, unemployment in Quebec under that government is considerably higher than it is in Ontario and on the prairies. I believe it was the late Mr. King who, on one occasion, made the classic statement that there would not be one five-cent piece for those provinces which did not have Liberal governments in office. Presumably this is an example of classical politics, Liberal version. In any case, there are different viewpoints on this question of responsibility.
The hon. member's next suggestion relates to the establishment of a council of economic advisers whose only function apparently would be to make reports. Surely, the national economic development board would make this suggestion obsolete, even before it gets off the drawing board.
The final suggestion made by the hon. member relates to an annual report. In summary, therefore, the suggestion before us boils down to this; a declaration of full employment policy by parliament; a declaration by no one knows who to the effect that the federal government is responsible; regular reports from the advisory board and an annual report by a minister. No matter how I look at this bill, Mr. Speaker, I cannot see it as a vehicle to provide jobs. It is not in a class with the municipal winter works program; the vocational school program, which is providing training facilities on a national scale; the manpower adjustment measure recently introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr); the Atlantic provinces development board which opposition members from the maritime provinces have been praising with such faint damns in the last few days, or the various other incentives and encouragements provided to industry and labour by this government.
As I say, it is a measure couched in vague generalities, embodying pious aspirations and hoping for the best. All I can say is that if we pass this bill at this time it would not result in one additional job for one single Canadian. Surely, that is the test. Let us not try to provide the public with window
Labour Conditions
dressing. Let us either put forward the kind of practical, positive steps as the government has been doing, and which the house has supported, or let us refrain from taking up time.
I commend the hon. member's idealism, but certainly I cannot commend his realism in the matter. In conclusion, may I also commend to the hon. member the views expressed by Dr. Eugene Forsey at the founding convention of his party on full employment and regimentation.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF MEASURE TO ENSURE FULL EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to make a few observations on the measure now before the house. At the outset, I should like to say that the objective I believe is in the mind of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is indeed very commendable. His objective is to realize the desirable goal when everyone will be assured the opportunity of gainful and productive employment. As we consider that objective I am sure, as the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, everyone in this house would agree with it. However, as we look at it there are a number of criticisms I should like to make, and I would make them I trust not in the spirit in which some criticisms have been levelled this afternoon. I want to make them as constructive as possible. I should like also to raise some questions with regard to the various sections that are in the motion.
The problem that faces us at the present time, a problem that has faced us over the years, causes us to consider the best methods and means by which we can assure the people of Canada the opportunity of gainful employment, to assure to them the possibility of meeting their own needs and the need of their families from an economic point of view. There are those who can look back to the years when this objective was far from possible even for the majority of Canadian citizens. Those were the years when dire poverty stalked the land, when the morale of the people was broken down because of their inability to provide for themselves and their families. I am sure that none of us anticipate a recurrence of the situation that faced us back in the thirties. Nevertheless, we are faced with a situation where, year after year, a considerable percentage of our people are unable to find productive and gainful employment.
I believe that this is wasteful when we consider the tremendous possibilities and the potential of this nation of ours. When we consider the needs of our people and the needs of other people, as has been pointed out by the hon. member who introduced this measure, we would say it is wasteful when people are unable to find an opportunity to

Labour Conditions
employ their time and their energy in productive enterprise, and make their contribution to society in the way they would like to make it. Not only is it wasteful but it is demoralizing as well, because I am still convinced that by far the greater percentage of Canadian people would rather provide for their own needs than have agencies, organizations or governments provide for them.
They are only asking for an opportunity to use their skills, their brawn and their brain to provide for themselves and for the needs of others. So I say that this bill before us now is commendable in that it points forward towards the realization of that goal when everyone will be assured of the opportunity of gainful and productive employment. However, I would raise a number of questions concerning the measure put forward to deal with the situation.
In the first clause, it suggests that there must be a clearcut recognition by parliament of the importance of full employment, in other words a national policy of full employment. I should like to ask the hon. member, what is full employment? What does he mean by full employment? In order to have full employment, is it required that everyone work so many days a week or so many hours in a day? Does full employment mean adequate work, sufficient work to enable a person to provide adequately for himself and others who are dependent upon him? Sometimes we refer to what we call the problem of automation. Unfortunately, so far as information is concerned at the present time, it would almost seem as though automation is the problem. I suggest that it should be a blessing when people can be relieved of the drudgery of manual labour and can spend at least a certain percentage of their time in cultural and other pursuits, developing their personalities, and making contributions not only in the field of economics but in the field of arts and so on. It seems to me this is a very desirable objective to attain.
In connection with the question of full employment I would like to ask what is full employment? As I said, is it so many days a week, so many hours in each day, or is it sufficient labour to produce the goods and services that are required with the workers receiving for themselves adequate returns commensurate with their contributions?
The next clause speaks about the role of the government and suggests-
-a declaration that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the steps that are necessary to provide and maintain a full employment economy.
I do not know just how far the hon. member would go in applying this particular

clause. He states that it is the responsibility of the government, but I do not believe it is the responsibility of government to give everyone a job. I do not believe it is the responsibility of the government to expand its services and engage in projects and all these different activities in order that it can employ more and more of the Canadian people. In contrast, I suggest the responsibility of parliament and of the government is to create a climate in this nation that will enable industry and business to move forward and produce the goods and services that are required in abundance sufficient to meet the needs of the people of Canada and of other nations. The responsibility of the government is to create an economic climate where business, industry and commerce can work and thereby provide gainful opportunities to the people of the nation.
The next clause in the motion speaks about the establishing of a council of economic advisers. The hon. member has indicated that he does not believe there would be any overlapping of responsibility between this and other activities that have already been considered in this house; but I would suggest that, in view of the fact we have so many other matters under consideration for setting up boards, commissions, committees and so on to consider these various factors, this would be a duplication of those other bodies. I just refer to one, the industrial change and manpower adjustment measure. The appointment of a council of advisers, such as indicated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would be a duplication of activities and interests that will' be considered with respect to that measure.
Once again we raise the question as to how many of these boards, commissions and committees we are going to have in order to get our economy moving and meet the changing situations of our nation. I do not think this council would be necessary in order to achieve the desirable objectives we have in mind.
So, Mr. Speaker, we support the principle of adequate employment for our people. We support the idea that everyone who desires it should have the opportunity and privilege of engaging in gainful employment. We agree with that; but so far as some of the measures that are proposed to reach that objective are concerned, we have some questions in our minds.
I come back once again to one of the basic proposals of our group. I know it has been raised on a number of occasions and so far it has not gained universal support, but we

still maintain that if we are to meet the challenges and problems facing us at the present time the government must accept responsibility to introduce measures to bring into being a financial system adequate to meet the changing situations as we find them today. That would require that adequate means be provided whereby purchasing power will be placed in the hands of the Canadian people, supplementary to wages and salaries, and that will bear a proper relationship to our production.
We believe and insist that if this were done, and goods and services moved to the people who require them, then we would achieve the objectives outlined by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; because if this is done, then the wheels of industry and production will continue in motion, more men will be employed, wages and salaries will continue to rise and all our people will share in the national prosperity. I do not raise these questions or issues in any critical manner. We believe the objective is good, but we have reservations with regard to the means that are being proposed to remedy the situation.

Labour Conditions
There are one or two other points I would like to deal with specifically. Some hon. members have already touched on them. One is paragraph (b) of the motion which suggests-
-a declaration that it is the responsibility of the federal government to take the steps that are necessary to provide and maintain a full employment economy.
I cannot help feeling that this particular section of the motion could not avoid running into constitutional difficulties at some time or another. It reminds me very much of a case back in the thirties, a very famous case before the Supreme Court of Canada, the labour convention case, where Canada agreed at an international convention to carry out certain reforms in the field of labour in Canada and then found, when the delegates came home, that they did not have the constitutional authority to do it because that power, of course, lies with the provinces. For this reason I feel that any catch-all bill, no matter how well intentioned it may be-and as this one undoubtedly is-dealing with the question of employment purely on a federal basis would run into that type of situation sooner or later, and very probably sooner.
There is another matter in paragraph (b) of the motion which has been discussed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, and that is the question of what is meant by full employment. Full employment is one of those catch-all terms that has become coined and used in our vocabulary in modern times. It is like "disarmament". Nobody can explain exactly what disarmament means, and likewise I do not think anybody can explain what full employment means. The committee resumed at 8 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, when you called it five o'clock, I had almost concluded my speech.
In the course of my remarks this afternoon, I insisted on the positive need for the two great races of our country to try to understand and know each other better.
It seems it would be relatively easy to find an answer to this dilemma if we could, through the setting up of a body, either here, within parliament, or outside this house, call upon experts in this field, both in the federal civil service and in the management of crown companies, to look carefully into all aspects of the participation of the two main racial groups of Canada in the administration of the country. The important thing is to find a simple formula which would enable us, precisely because of its simplicity, to settle this matter promptly and definitely from all points of view.
In my opinion, the whole matter should be considered immediately, because the uneasiness resulting throughout Canada from the differences that separate us, we of French Canada from our fellow citizens of English Canada, threatens to grow rapidly to disastrous proportions for our way of life.
Mr. Chairman, during the campaign which preceded the election of June 18 last, it was easy to realize that a feeling of concern existed among the people in general. Through interviews on radio and television, the public was consulted in relation to that problem, because it was of interest to all voters. To the questions "What is your interest in this federal election? What do you expect from the party that will be elected on June 18 next?" Quebec voters answered three times out of five and perhaps more often; In the first place, we want national unity to become a reality; we want a distinct national flag under which we can unite; we want a national anthem about which we can become enthu-

Interim Supply
siastic; we want some way to get along better, to understand each other better.
In fact, this only confirmed a personal opinion I have had for some time because some ten months before the general election I had a fairly thorough survey of public opinion made by very responsible friends in my own riding. In that survey, I asked the question: "What do you expect from the federal government?" And most voters in my riding, who represented more or less all classes of voters to be found in any urban riding, had in fact answered that what interested them most of all was the adoption of distinctive symbols which could give the Canadian nation its sovereignty and at the same time provide for that better understanding which is asked for nowadays.
That is why I believe that the solution to this problem is that we, the federal government, must consider it with the provincial authorities. Furthermore, it will have to be studied through a simple body to be established here by the federal government and which will find the necessary formula to study all its aspects in order to find the formula so much desired and so desirable. In that way, we shall learn to know each other better and thereby we shall have more consideration for each other.
Mr. Chairman, there is in Canada something incomprehensible. As a matter of fact, if we take a look at what happened to our mighty neighbour to the south, we find that Americans, whatever their ethnic origin, whether they be of English, French, Italian, Jewish or other descent, have all rallied around the symbols of national sovereignty and to everybody who asks, they say: "I am an American." That does not mean that they have lost the characteristics one relates to their respective origins. But one thing is certain. They have all assembled around those symbols, whatever part of the country they may come from. Indeed, they are Americans first and foremost, that is before being loyal to their land of origin.
It is essential that this extraordinary unity and this national pride which exist among our neighbours to the south, both of which have made them so powerful, be found here in our country. It is worthy of note that, at this moment, all members of this house, be they from the government party to which I belong, from the Liberal opposition to which the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) belongs, or from the Social Credit opposition to which the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) belongs, are trying to unite, to

join forces and to find a formula which, by going above and beyond political partisanship, will indeed become a formula for national patriotism, a formula which will enable all Canadians to develop and prosper; in short, a formula which will perhaps do away, once and for all, with each and every one of those unfortunate dissensions which have hurt us in the past, which threaten us now and which must be eliminated for the best interests of the Canadian nation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
All of us in this House of Commons cannot but welcome the statement made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. He dealt with a very important issue. He dealt with it in a thoughtful and constructive manner. I would say that we also welcome the response which has been made by the Associate Minister of National Defence. I dare to hope that, as a result of this kind of thoughtful discussion of an important problem, we can make some headway in dealing with it.
We, as members of the New Democratic party, support wholeheartedly the proposition that every effort must be made to establish mutual respect and equality between the two great races that brought this country into being. We feel that it is not only a matter of according rights and adjusting certain grievances that have grown up, but that it will add to the richness of life in this country if we can further the binational, bieultural and biethnical heritage which is already ours. This was the position this party took at its founding convention in the summer of 1961. I am happy to remind hon. members that a few months later the leader of the New Democratic party, my colleague the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, called for the appointment of a royal commission to study all aspects of this feature of our national life.
I say again that we welcome speeches of the kind made this afternoon. We hope this indicates we are turning a bit of a corner with regard to this problem and that instead of its being one about which nasty things are said, it might be one to which we shall apply our constructive efforts.
I rose to take part in this debate, however, intending to base what I had to say mainly on the words used by the Minister of Finance when he opened this debate on December 12. The words in question are to be found at page 2590 of Hansard of that date, at which time the minister said:
Mr. Chairman, I can give the usual assurance which all ministers of finance give at this time,

that the passing of this hill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of hon. members to criticize any item of the estimates when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and the usual undertaking that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.
Let me read again the last few words of that undertaking given by the Minister of Finance:
-such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.
I am fully satisfied that the Minister of Finance gave that undertaking in good faith. I am fully satisfied that when he gave it he meant it. I am equally satisfied that this undertaking will not be kept. I make the flat prediction that this fiscal year 1962-63 will pass without our having the opportunity to deal with the estimates, a portion of which we are now being asked to vote by way of interim supply. I suggest that this is more than just a procedural point. This is something which is leading into a crisis, so far as the operations of the parliament of Canada are concerned.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out in an opening sentence this afternoon we are, in this interim supply bill, being asked to vote the tenth twelfth of the revised and supplementary estimates for the fiscal year 1962-63. At this point, however, we have not voted in committee of supply a single one of the main, revised or supplementary estimates. This money we are now voting is for the month of January.
This Thursday night at ten o'clock we are supposed to adjourn for a Christmas recess. We do not meet again until Monday, January 21. By that time we shall be approaching the month of February and it is inevitable that, within a few days after we return, the Minister of Finance will come down with another interim supply bill in which he will seek money for the month of February, 1963. In that instance he will be asking for the eleventh twelfth of the estimates before this House of Commons, and in all probability at that point we shall still be exactly where we are now in that not a single item of the estimates themselves will have been passed. On that occasion no doubt he will again give us the assurance that the passing of that interim supply bill will not curtail or restrict our right to discuss the main estimates.
However, Mr. Chairman, even if the House of Commons is not dissolved and an election is not brought on, even if we stay here, the weeks of February will come swiftly

Interim Supply
and before we know it we shall be approaching the end of that month, and we shall be faced with the question of whether or not we are going to give the government its twelfth twelfth of the year's estimates.
At that point other questions will arise. At what stage shall we be with respect to the estimates as a whole?
As hon. members are aware, the rules of this House of Commons require that in each session of parliament there shall be six supply motions with Mr. Speaker in the chair. Unless all six of those motions are put, debated and carried, it is not possible to get all of the main estimates opened in committee of supply. Thus far we have had only one supply motion in this session of parliament. It will take five more supply motions, each of which can be debated for two days, just to get the departments of the government opened in committee of supply. It takes no expert calculation to realize that, in the light of that situation, it is utterly impossible to get the estimates passed before the end of February in order to vote the supply bill, or before the time will come when the minister will want his twelfth twelfth.
What is this house going to do when that point is reached? I hear noises from across the way that this is the last time the Social Credit group is going to vote for an interim supply bill unless, of course, the government does certain things in the meantime. But I say to my hon. friends across the way, despite their saying that they are not going to vote further money, I say this to the Liberals and I say to all of us that the point gets reached where parliament is boxed in. The point gets reached where the administration of the affairs of the country has to carry on. Salaries have to be paid and the withholding of the actual money to carry on the essential services of the government is something that this parliament may find it is impossible to do.
So what happens when that point is reached? I suggest that either one of two things will happen. Either the government will come before us with some kind of omnibus bill asking us to vote all the estimates in one swift action because by then the government will argue it is time to start talking about the estimates for 1963-64, or because parliament stands on its feet and because parliament seeks to debate these items there will either be prorogation of the session so the government can use governor general's warrants or there will be dissolution and an election. I do not know which of these various courses is going to be followed, but I do know that no matter which one of them is pursued we are going to witness the fiscal year 1962-63 as one in which parliament and

Interim Supply
the House of Commons in particular did not have its traditional, its constitutional right to discuss the items in the estimates as the Minister of Finance on December 12 assured us we would have. Not because there was anything lacking in the assurance he gave, but rather because of the time that has been taken with a long summer interval when there was no session of parliament and the failure of the government to organize the business of this session, we are going to be in the position where one of the main rights that is supposed to belong to parliament will have been lost.
That main right to which I am referring is parliament's control over the purse strings. That is what we are supposed to have, not the kind of government in which the executive makes all the decisions and spends all the money but the kind of government we are supposed to have is one in which, whatever else the executive may be able to do by order in council, by executive action, control of the purse remains with parliament itself. We are going to lose that control in this fiscal year 1962-63 either by the passage of time or by dissolution and an election.
I submit that this is more than what some people sometimes call just a procedural question, and it is more than just a political question with regard to whether or not there is going to be an election. I submit that this is a serious situation which points up that the authority and the rights of parliament are being downgraded, are being whittled away, by the way in which things have been going in the last little while, particularly in this session.
I have taken the trouble to spell out what is happening to us in terms of the estimates to portray what I believe to be the situation we face, in that we are getting to the point where the government of this country is entirely an executive operation rather than something in which the authority of parliament really plays its part. This, Mr. Chairman, is just one phase of this session which points up the fact, but I submit it points it up very dramatically. If we go on, if we get another of these supply bills for an eleventh twelfth and another for a twelfth twelfth, it will be pointed up so that everyone in the country will be able to see that parliament's control of the purse strings has been taken away.
This is not the only thing that has happened in this session. We have had difficulties regarding a budget, and just as I said that we would go through the fiscal year 1962-63 without a full discussion of the estimates-in fact, we may go through without finally voting any estimate in committee of supply-so we shall go through the year 1962-63 without

a formal budget debate, without an opportunity to discuss in the traditional way the budgetary policies of the government of this country. I need not spell it out at length because we have done so on other occasions when we have had the opportunity, but some of us feel that even the power to impose taxation has been taken away from parliament and exercised by the executive because of the way in which customs surcharges were imposed on June 24 by an order in council.
What I am underlining in all of these things, Mr. Chairman, if I may use the same language again, is that it is not just a matter of a point of order being got around, but rather that what is happening is that the authority of parliament, the place of parliament in the government of this country, is being downgraded. This very debate is one that is bringing out the frustrations that this session of parliament has experienced. We had a very interesting speech the other day by the hon. member for St. Antoine-West-mount on the subject of national defence. Whether or not one agrees with his conclusions is another thing, but the point is he had to choose this debate on interim supply to have a discussion on this subject, and no doubt before this debate is over others will make a contribution to that subject. This simply turns the searchlight on the fact that in this critical time in our nation's history, in this critical time in the world's history, the parliament of Canada has been given no proper opportunity to discuss defence policy or external relations.
This afternoon on motions we had a bit of a discussion when the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke on his trip to NATO and there were comments from the leaders of the other three parties. Then we had attempts on the orders of the day to get certain information about nuclear policy and other aspects of external policy. But here we are, Mr. Chairman, in the third month of this session of parliament without parliament itself having had any opportunity to discuss these terribly important questions of defence policy and external policy. Even the chances we have to question the ministers are very limited and the answers that we get, for example the answers the Prime Minister gave today, suggest that somehow or other this government feels that this is an executive preserve. The government will make the decisions and when announcements are made, be they announcements of policy or changes in policy, they will be made known to the house and to the country.
We are not in the kind of state, Mr. Chairman, where a small group is elected to run things. We have a parliamentary form of

government. This country elects 265 people to be their representatives, to be their parliament, to which the government is responsible. Yet opportunities tor discussion of important matters such as I have just named, estimates, a budget, taxation, external affairs, defence, have been completely denied to this first session of this twenty fifth parliament. Rumours that are flying around suggest that anything could happen, that parliament itself could end without anything of this sort having been discussed. Even if parliament does not end, to come back to the prediction I made earlier, we are going to see ourselves going through the fiscal year 1962-63 without parliament really being in the picture so far as these issues are concerned. Oh, we have a government and the government is making decisions. The government is passing orders in council. The government is staying in power. The government is keeping things going. But this, Mr. Chairman, has the effect of downgrading parliament, robbing parliament of its authority, of the role it is supposed to play in the life of our country.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this issue is bigger than the question of which party is in power. My hon. friends of the Liberal party do not need to sit back and enjoy the fact that perhaps I am roasting the present government a bit, because when they were on the government side their record was not too good on the subject of maintaining the authority of parliament. When they had something they wanted to put through their motto was, who can stop us? What I am complaining about is that the damage the Liberals did to parliament is not over. This attitude, who can stop us, is still with us. We still have a government that is acting by executive authority and treats parliament as a nuisance, a debating society that has to be called into session but which has to be kept from making any decisions on major matters such as estimates, the budget, external policy, defence policy and so on.
And taxation.

Let me go on. During the last four or five years some of us believe this government made significant and serious changes in policy regarding two crown corporations, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Trans-Canada Air Lines. We do not like the changes in policy that the government made during the years 1957 to 1962. On June 18, 1962, there was an election and the government that had been in power for the last four years with a clear majority received a minority of the popular vote. I do not suggest
Interim Supply
that everybody who voted against the government disagreed with it on every matter of policy that was before the country at that time. I do suggest that the policy pursued by the government in at least those two areas, the question of what is being done to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the question of what is being done to Trans-Canada Air Lines, should not continue to be pursued wtihout being discussed in parliament.
Have we had any opportunity of discussing questions relating to radio and television broadcasting? Have we had any opportunity of discussing questions relating to the air policy of this government or to transportation policy in general? Oh, questions have been asked on orders of the day. The reports of the Canadian National Railways and Trans-Canada Air Lines have been before the committee on railways, air lines and shipping. There have been one or two little bills regarding branch lines; but in the main, so far as policies affecting these two areas of our national life are concerned, there has been no opportunity to discuss them at all.
We think what is being done to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is bad for Canada. We think it was one of the things which, before it was interfered with by the recent changes, was something of which we could be proud as a nation. It was something distinctively Canadian. It was something that added to our sense of national unity. The extent to which recent changes of policy have changed that picture alarm us. At this point I am trying to debate the issue, Mr. Chairman, or any of these issues. I am simply making the point that no opportunity to discuss these matters has come before this house.
My hon. friend who interrupted me, if I heard him correctly, says that we can discuss them now. Of course, we can discuss anything now, and that is what is happening in this debate. This is the reason this debate on interim supply which was started last Wednesday, the kind of debate that sometimes takes a couple of hours, is already now in its fourth day and may go two or three more. We have had no opportunity to discuss these things in the way in which parliament can express itself in terms of making decisions. The Columbia river situation has been brought into the debate because the government has failed to bring the treaty before parliament. Hon. members have had to take advantage of this debate to discuss that subject. The question of investigations by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police has been raised because we have had no chance to discuss it in a formal way so that decisions could be made. We have had to discuss that subject in this debate on interim supply.

Interim Supply
I do not know how many other questions may yet be raised before this debate on the granting of the tenth twelfth of interim supply is completed. All of this, Mr. Chairman, as I say could be classed as a procedural complaint. People may say, as some member did a moment ago, we can talk now if we want to do so. What it points up is that this is a sterile session of parliament in which we can talk the number of hours that are allotted to us but in which we are being denied the right to make decisions on matters that are of real concern.
One of the matters that is concerning Canada today is the whole question of health and health services. I know there are some members who thought that at the time a certain battle was taking place last summer interest in this whole question would subside. However, interest in it has grown since then, instead of subsiding. The fact of the matter is that in this session of parliament we have had no chance to discuss health insurance or the related subject of social security. I have tried on orders of the day to raise the question of what is happening in respect of the proposed amendment to the British North America Act to provide for contributory pensions. I think I have the record for monosyllabic answers; I get yes or no to this or that. We have had correspondence tabled, but it all adds up to a pretty clear indication that nothing is going to be done at this session in the important field or social security. We have a motion on the order paper which will not be reached. After all, only eight of the provinces have agreed to it and at least one of the provinces, perhaps more, suggested that if you cannot get this amendment through at least do something about raising the old age pension from its present level to $75 per month or some such figure as was promised in the election campaign.
Do we get a chance to discuss this? Do we get these things brought before us? No, we get the stock answer from the Prime Minister and other ministers of the government, if and when government policy is decided upon it will be announced in the house. It all adds up to this body of 265 men and women elected by the people of Canada to represent them here, the body to which the government is responsible, being just a debating forum. The newspapers are doing that; radio and television are holding their forums. These things are taking place. Indeed, the same job is being done that we are doing here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I must inform him his time has expired.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Chairman; I should like to come back later. Meantime, I hope something will be done to restore to parliament its authority.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, listening to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, we could not help thinking that he was just repeating what we have been saying in the house since last September. He took half an hour to do that.
Before coming to the point of my remarks, I feel it is my duty to express, oni behalf of the members of this group and of all hon. members, our most sincere condolences to the families of the two policemen who were shot down in Ville St. Laurent. Notorious bandits, disguised as Santa Claus, cold-bloodedly shot down at close range officers Claude Marineau and Denis Brabant while they were on duty. It will be a sad Christmas indeed for the wives and six children of the two murdered policemen.
After such barbarism in a Canadian city, namely Ville St. Laurent, I wonder what some hon. members think now of the abolition of capital punishment.
On many occasions, we have heard urgent pleas for the abolition of capital punishment for murderers. And yet, in Montreal, a few days ago, that is last Friday, December 14, four notorious bandits killed two policemen on duty.
I congratulate the federal authorities as well as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) for maintaining the death penalty in Canada, to punish that kind of people, those despicable individuals who go about not only in the city of Montreal, but also in Toronto, and elsewhere in Canada, and against whom there is no protection. The government is well-advised to protect society against such individuals.
The murders committed last week are of a kind to rouse to indignation the whole population, and we should of course take steps to prevent the recurrence of such crimes.
Mr. Chairman, I have said enough on this matter. I believe the members of this house are unanimous in their desire to offer their condolences to both bereaved families and particularly to the children who will always bear in their mind the picture of Santa Claus killing their father. Let us have a thought for them and let us hope that such

terrifying things will not occur again within our borders or in any of our provinces.
Mr. Chairman, this afternoon, I listened to the magnificent contributions of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), who reiterated in this house what has been said in many instances over the years.
I commend those who contributed to the discussion this afternoon, because they kept the debate free of any partisan and political considerations.
The Social Credit group in this house will do all it can to help achieve any measure of Canadian unity-that understanding between the two great Canadian cultures-without using it as a political football.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, members of all parties have kept the discussion, this afternoon and tonight, above those partisan and political questions. Indeed, I believe that the Leader of the Opposition delivered this afternoon his best speech since he went into active politics.
In recent months, I had the opportunity of visiting all Canadian provinces. I was surprised to find as much among my Anglo-Saxon and English Canadian fellow citizens as among French Canadians, a wish, even a need, to feel joined and united together. I went to British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, and Ontario, and especially in the province of Ontario, which was described throughout Canada as an inaccessible province, I was able to meet 2,000 students of the University of Toronto. I also met members of the Ontario junior chamber of commerce, in Toronto more exactly, who were tactful enough to introduce me in French to an all-English audience. How pleasant it is for a French Canadian to go to Toronto and to be introduced in his mother tongue to his English speaking fellow citizens who do not understand perhaps a single word of French. I also had the opportunity of meeting 300 or 400 young engineers in Toronto. Last week, I met colleagues from Sales Advertising, in Guelph, about 60 miles from Toronto, and there again the master of ceremonies was glad to introduce me in my own language, in French.
As a colleague, the hon. member for Lapointe said this afternoon, French Canadians are looking for and want a real understanding in Canada. They are not French Canadians, no, they are Canadians. They are Canadians who recognize the existence of the two cultures which enabled Canada to be
Interim, Supply
what it is today, what it will be tomorrow, what it will be in the future if this understanding between the two cultures exists in this country of ours.
I would blame myself if, at this stage, I did not congratulate the government of Ontario from the bottom of my heart, for introducing a bill which provides for the teaching of French in Ontario schools at a higher grade than was the case only a few weeks ago. Recently, I met people from western Canada-people of 45 or 50 years of age who told me quite frankly that, if 30 years ago somebody had suggested they learn French, they would never have done so, but who today regret not having learned it. Well, even at that time, we, in our own province, were glad to learn English from the second or third grades, that is from the time we were seven or eight years old, so that, at the age of 20, 25, 30 or 35, we could go anywhere in Canada and express ourselves in the mother tongue of other Canadians in any province.
We are proud of this achievement and we are convinced that English Canadians would get exactly the same satisfaction if they had done the same, and my own conviction is based on the reception given me all across Canada.
We want a united Canada and the closer we are together, as this great country of ours pursues its destiny, the better can this mutual understanding on a national scale become a reality.
As the Leader of the Opposition was saying this afternoon, we have been misunderstood by English speaking Canadians. French Canadians have been misunderstood.
In the province of Quebec, as we all know, the Anglo-Saxons, the English speaking Canadians receive exactly the same treatment as the French Canadians, in every respect: education, church, public assistance to schools, etc.
In the city of Montreal, English speaking Canadians are treated exactly the same as French Canadians, and it is the same in Quebec city, or in Rouyn-Noranda, where I live.
That is what we are asking for: that same understanding all across Canada. To that end, we suggest, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) indicated this afternoon, the setting up of a department of federal-provincial affairs which would allow provincial authorities to meet and to know each other better.

Interim Supply
We realize that in this very House of Commons, because when French and English speaking Canadians meet here, they get along perfectly well together. The same thing could be carried out on a national basis for the welfare of the whole Canadian population, and not only in one particular part of the country.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, the Social Crediters want to do their share without playing politics. I repeat what I said at the outset of my remarks, not to play politics. I repeat that all parties have kept above partisan considerations because we recognize that before being Liberals, Conservatives N.D.P.'s or Social Crediters, we are Canadians and it is as Canadians that we are responsible to the people we represent here in this House of Commons.
Mr. Chairman, national unity and friendly understanding can come true. All we need is good will, and my deep conviction is that we shall succeed.
We had our failures in the past. True, we have played politics instead of trying to understand each other. However, we were not so successful in achieving the purpose of our existence as Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, there have been internal divisions in the past between one racial group and another. That was mostly due to our economic system which prevented one group from developing and progressing at the same rate as the other. Both groups suffered from exactly the same misgivings, made the same mistakes and lacked the same things.
It is no use talking about unity which cannot be realized, but there is one sphere in which we can achieve unity, that is the economic sphere. Everyone including the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, and indeed, all members of parliament, have heard it said throughout the Canadian provinces that 80 per cent of our economy is in the hands of foreigners while we control the remaining 20 per cent.
Yet, it is the Canadian people who are working and building. Canadian materials and products are being used for the development of our country and no solution is being found. We have solutions for practically any problem. We tackle all kinds of problems but we are doing nothing about the most important problem of all, that of money and credit in Canada.
A few days ago, an hon. member of this house set out to attack Social Credit, as if

one could expect anything else. I am speaking about my friend, the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) who accused the Prime Minister of acting-
-in complicity, now with the Social Credit party mostly, now with the New Democratic party.
He added:
It is shameful all the same, Mr. Chairman, to act in collusion with a political party which merely wants to lead our country to ruin-
There, he wanted to name Social Credit, but he was a bit shy.
Mr. Chairman, I see the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) applauding, without quite knowing why. It is a habit of hers.
-without its having the courage to inform the population sufficiently on its policy of crazy money-
Mr. Chairman, I underline the words "crazy money", because the hon. member refused to do it.
-its system of dividends for all-
That is funny. A system of taxes for all, that is more serious, of course. A system of money, enough money to kill, that is logical. A system of money to enable everybody to make a living, that is funny, that makes people laugh, especially the member for Beauharnois-Salaberry. He will have the people in his own riding laughing at him with that.
-its system of dividends for all, as long as the money machine holds out.
The money machine must be allowed to keep on working.
Everybody thought it was funny to hear about the monkey in the banana tree, the worm in the apple, the hare or the rabbit in the hollow log.
That was funny-to watch a monkey die from hunger.
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. I just want to thank the hon. member for Villeneuve for repeating my speech. I appreciate it very much.

Mr. Chairman, it was not a point of order but rather a question of privilege. I am satisfied because he may not remember what he said.
Mr. Chairman, to see a monkey die from hunger in a banana tree, because there are too many bananas, that is funny. But, on the other hand, to see children, human beings, adults, in some lanes in the city of Montreal, and maybe even in the riding of my hon.

friend from Beauharnois-Salaberry, going through the garbage pails, behind restaurants, to pick up scraps of food because they do not have the right, like the financiers, to go and buy in stores, that is not funny. It is serious, and no doubt that happens in my hon. friend's riding.
But to speak of a monkey that dies from hunger in a banana tree, of a rabbit that runs from one end of a log to the other, that is funny.
And I continue:
It was funny to hear about the stomach of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and that of the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), without forgetting the head of the member for Port Arthur which should be cut off for the sake of better planning with regard to the leader of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas).
And a little further down, the hon. member stated:
Do you think those people are serious? Is the hon. Prime Minister himself serious? The people of Canada are surely not being fooled. The Social Crediters must hide their real selves under the cloak of nationalism-
Quite apt.

Mr. Chairman, I just heard the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger) who said "Quite apt". He saw me in my own constituency when I met businessmen. At that time, we were discussing Social Credit, we were discussing monetary reforms. Now, the reforms which are a must at present are as important as the replacement of some hon. members. The monetary reform is still of the utmost importance throughout the country, and that is why the Social Crediters believe in it and preach it across the province and the whole of Canada.
You were not elected on the Social Credit platform.
You bet I was.
Not at all.

It is a fact that we explained Social Credit. If the hon. member had listened to the radio and television, he might have understood a few things. Maybe he does not have the possibility of understanding, but his constituents in Beauharnois-Salaberry understand very well.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order. The hon. member for Villeneuve says that the Social Credit members were elected after they explained the Social Credit doctrine. That was not the way they were elected at all. They promised $100 a month.

They knew they could never succeed in giving such an amount, because they will never
be called upon to form the government.
